The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior. 
Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically manages how runs and chunks are placed on GPUs, 
freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work. 

As the above figure shows, with suitable IC Ops based on the runs' learning behaviors, you are 
able to compare 9 configs in roughly the same time it took to compare 3 sequentially! 
:doc:`Read more about IC Ops here</icops>`.

.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu2.png
   :width: 800px

In the second example shown above, we show how you can be even more aggressive with your 
exploration thanks to RapidFire AI: launching 8 configs together even on just 1 GPU. 
And with multiple Stop and Clone-Modify operations, you can get a feel for even 14 configs 
on 1-2 shards each in roughly the time it would take to compare just 2 configs on the full data! 
All the while, you are free to continue the training of whichever configs still look promising, 
resume those that you had stopped earlier, clone the clones further, and so on.

Types of Metrics
-----------------------

We support 2 types of metrics based on their aggregation semantics: 

* **Distributive Metrics:** These are purely additive over a given set of data points. 
  
  Examples: *count* of number of correct predictions; *sum* of output token lengths across queries.

* **Algebraic Metrics:** These are averages or proportions over a given set of data points. They can be decomposed into components that are individually distributive. 
  
  Examples: *precision*, which counts number of correct predictions and total number of data points separately and then divides them; *mean rouge-1*, which averages per-example rouge-1 values that assesses overlap of tokens between generated text and ground truth text.

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

This means you get **running metric estimates with confidence intervals** in real time. 
So, you can confidently stop poor configs earlier, clone better configs on the fly, and 
perform more informed exploration to reach much better eval metrics in much less time.

Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here. 
:doc:`As also explained on this page</difference>`, downsampling alone has 
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually 
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files. 
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated 
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.

RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach with IC Ops avoids all the above issues,
while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in 
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.

One clone is then stopped halfway through the aggregation, while the other two run to completion. 
Ultimately, the other clone ends up being the best config overall.

Note that the confidence intervals shown will keep narrowing as configs see more shards, converging 
to zero when 100% of the data is seen, i.e., the metrics become exact point estimates.
Overall, compared to sequential batch evals in which the original 4 configs all run to completion, 
RapidFire AI enables you to explore more configs in less time, while reaching better eval metrics.



Types of Metrics
-----------------------

We support 2 types of metrics based on their aggregation semantics: 

* **Distributive Metrics:** These are purely additive over a given set of data points. 
  
  Examples: *count* of number of correct predictions; *sum* of output token lengths across queries.

* **Algebraic Metrics:** These are averages or proportions over a given set of data points. They can be decomposed into components that are individually distributive. 
  
  Examples: *precision*, which counts number of correct predictions and total number of data points separately and then divides them; *mean rouge-1*, which averages per-example rouge-1 values that assesses overlap of tokens between generated text and ground truth text.

reference_answer: RapidFire AI generalizes hyperparameter sweep ideas to many types of config knobs. Beyond regular hyperparameters, it can vary base model architectures, prompt schemes, LoRA adapters, optimizers for training, and RAG choices such as data chunking, embeddings, retrieval, reranking, generation, prompt schemes, and other user-defined knobs.

Range() accepts a start value, an end value, and a dtype that is either "int" or "float". The documentation states that, as of this writing, Range() performs uniform sampling within the given interval.

The documentation recommends explicitly ending a previous experiment before starting a new one so users remain aware of code or config changes across experiments. It also notes that if a Jupyter kernel restarts or is interrupted, rerunning the constructor cell can reconnect to and continue the existing experiment unless it was explicitly ended.

The param_config argument to run_fit() can be a single config dictionary, a list of config dictionaries, a config group generator output such as RFGridSearch() or RFRandomSearch(), or a list mixing configs and config group generator outputs.

For run_evals(), num_shards is identical in purpose to run_fit()'s num_chunks. It balances the degree of concurrency for cross-config comparisons against minor swapping overhead, and the docs again recommend at least 4 so results update for all runs on one fourth of the data at a time.

RFLangChainRagSpec wraps LangChain APIs for the pre-generator stages of a RAG pipeline. It specifies data loading, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and reranking, with many of these stages being optional.

Document Preprocessing workers operate in parallel over the base data to produce preprocessed data stored in a vector store. Query Processing workers operate over eval examples by embedding queries, retrieving relevant chunks, reranking them, constructing context, and generating outputs.

RFLangChainRagSpec defines create, read, and update modes. Create mode builds a new vector store when a document loader is provided without pre-existing index or collection names. Read mode opens a pre-existing index or collection when no document loader is provided. Update mode adds new documents to an existing index or collection when both a document loader and pre-existing names are provided.

FAISS uses a flat L2 index by default and is an in-memory store, so it only supports create mode and does not have pre-existing indexes. Pinecone supports create, read, and update workflows with pre-existing index and namespace pairs required for read or update mode.

get_context() accepts batch_queries plus two options: use_reranker and serialize. use_reranker controls whether a configured reranker is applied and defaults to true. serialize controls whether retrieved documents are returned as formatted strings or raw Document objects, and also defaults to true.

RFPromptManager wraps LangChain APIs for dynamic few-shot example selection. It uses semantic similarity-based example selection to construct prompts with the examples most relevant to each input query.

The FiQA preprocessing example retrieves unserialized documents with rag.get_context(..., serialize=False), then extracts the corpus_id metadata field from each retrieved Document. It stores those IDs in retrieved_documents while separately serializing the retrieved documents for prompt construction.

The multimodal preprocessing example retrieves unserialized documents, extracts base64 image strings from each document's image_data metadata field, serializes text context separately, and builds user prompt content containing both a text block and image_url blocks for non-empty base64 images.

eval.compute_metrics_fn should return a dictionary whose keys are metric names. Each metric maps to another dictionary that must contain the reserved key "value" with that metric's value over the batch.

The sample create_model function reads model_name, model_type, and model_kwargs from model_config. It uses AutoModelForCausalLM for causal_lm, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM for seq2seq_lm, AutoModelForMaskedLM for masked_lm, allows custom loading logic for custom, and defaults to causal LM otherwise; it then loads the tokenizer with AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained().

A formatting function prepares each dataset row into the prompt and completion format expected by the model. It should return a dictionary with prompt and completion keys, each containing lists of chat messages with role and content fields.
Every reward function should return a list of floats, one per completion. It may also return None for examples where the reward function is not applicable, which is useful for multi-task training.

RFLoraConfig is a wrapper around Hugging Face PEFT's LoraConfig. The key difference is that individual arguments can be List-valued or Range-valued so they can define a base set of knob combinations for a config group.

RFModelConfig abstracts and unifies multiple Hugging Face APIs for model-related specifications. It brings together model loading, training configurations, LoRA settings, adapter structures, formatting and metrics functions, and generation specifics in one RapidFire API class.

The trainer example uses List([2e-4, 1e-5]) for learning_rate and List(["linear", "cosine"]) for lr_scheduler_type. The surrounding settings, such as batch sizes, epoch count, logging steps, eval strategy, eval steps, fp16, and save strategy, are shown as fixed values in that example.
Both SFT FSDP examples use full_shard auto_wrap with transformer-based wrapping. The larger tutorial example sets offload_params to False, while the lite tutorial example sets offload_params to True.

The DPO trainer example varies beta with List([0.1, 0.001]). The rest of the shown base_dpo_config includes settings such as model_adapter_name, ref_adapter_name, max prompt and completion lengths, batch size, optimizer, scheduler, and save strategy.

RFvLLMModelConfig recommends listing model, dtype, distributed_executor_backend, and max_model_len in model_config. The distributed executor backend can be ray or multiprocessing, with only multiprocessing supported for now, and max_model_len is automatically derived from the model config if unspecified.

As more shards are processed, the confidence intervals narrow and converge to zero when the full dataset has been processed. At that point, the metrics become exact point estimates over the full dataset.

The example compares 16 RAG configs on 400 queries split into 8 shards at 10 seconds per query on one machine. Traditional batch evals take 17.8 hours, while RapidFire AI's IC Ops workflow takes 3.8 hours by stopping weak configs early, adding variants, and continuing only the best config. The documented result is a 4.7x runtime cut, with token spend on closed-model APIs redirected toward more productive configs.

**`get_context()`** is governed by three user‑controlled options:

| Option | What it does | Default |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| **`use_reranker`** (bool) | If a `reranker_cfg` is present in the RAG spec, this flag decides whether the reranker is applied to the retrieved chunks. Set to `False` to skip reranking; `True` (default) runs the reranker. | `True` |
| **`serialize`** (bool) | Determines the return type. `True` (default) returns a list of formatted strings (chunks joined by double newlines). `False` returns the raw `Document` objects for each query. | `True` |
| **`reranker_cfg`** (dict) | The actual reranker configuration (e.g., `CrossEncoderReranker` with its `model_name`, `model_kwargs`, `top_n`, etc.). If this dict is omitted, no reranking is performed regardless of `use_reranker`. | *None* (no reranking) |

In short, **output format** is controlled by `serialize`, and **reranking behavior** is controlled by the presence of `reranker_cfg` together with the `use_reranker` flag.

RFPromptManager **wraps around LangChain APIs** and its role is to **manage dynamic few‑shot prompting** by selecting examples based on semantic similarity, constructing prompts that contain the most relevant examples for each input query.

In the FiQA preprocessing example the document IDs are kept in the **metadata** of each retrieved `Document`:

1. **Ingestion** – the `metadata_func` supplied to the `DirectoryLoader` (used in the `RFLangChainRagSpec`) stores the ID as `{"corpus_id": int(record.get("_id"))}` on every document.  
2. **Retrieval** – `rag.get_context(batch_queries=…, serialize=False)` returns a list of `Document` objects for each query.  
3. **Extraction** – the preprocess function reads the ID from each document’s metadata:

```python
retrieved_documents = [
    [doc.metadata["corpus_id"] for doc in docs]   # one list per query
    for docs in all_context
]
```

These `retrieved_documents` (lists of `corpus_id`s) are then passed downstream for evaluation.

The multimodal preprocess function first pulls the **un‑serialized** documents for each query (`rag.get_context(..., serialize=False)`) so it can read both the text and any image metadata that was stored during ingestion (e.g., `metadata["image_data"]` containing a base64 string).  

It then:

1. **Extracts the images** – builds a list‑of‑lists of base64 strings by reading `doc.metadata.get("image_data", "")` for every document returned for a query.  
2. **Serializes the text** – calls `rag.serialize_documents(all_context)` to get the plain‑text context that will go into the prompt’s text block.  
3. **Creates a multimodal prompt** – combines the serialized text block with an image‑content block (using the extracted base64 strings) in the prompt dictionary that is passed to the generator model.

Thus, image information is added to the generator prompts by pulling base64‑encoded image data from document metadata, keeping it separate from the serialized text, and inserting both as distinct content blocks in the final prompt.

The sample `create_model` function looks at the **`model_type`** entry in the supplied `model_config` dictionary and selects a Hugging Face class with a simple `if/elif/else` chain:

| `model_type` value | Hugging Face class instantiated |
|--------------------|---------------------------------|
| `"causal_lm"`      | `AutoModelForCausalLM` |
| `"seq2seq_lm"`     | `AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM` |
| `"masked_lm"`      | `AutoModelForMaskedLM` |
| `"custom"`         | user‑defined loading logic (placeholder) |
| *any other value* | defaults to `AutoModelForCausalLM` |

The chosen class is then called with `from_pretrained(model_name, **model_kwargs)`. The tokenizer is always created with `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)`.

A formatting function must return a **dictionary** with two keys:

* **`"prompt"`** – a list of message dictionaries, each containing a `"role"` (e.g., `"system"` or `"user"`) and a `"content"` string.  
* **`"completion"`** – a list of message dictionaries, each with a `"role"` (typically `"assistant"`) and a `"content"` string.

In type terms the return is `Dict[str, List[Dict[str, str]]]`. This structure supplies the prompt‑completion pair in the chat‑message format expected by the fine‑tuning trainer.

A GRPO reward function must return **either**

* a **list of floats** – one reward score for each generated completion, or  
* **`None`** – to indicate the reward is not applicable for that example (e.g., in multi‑task training).

**RFLoraConfig** is a thin wrapper around Hugging Face PEFT’s **`LoraConfig`**.  
The only functional extension it adds for RapidFire experiments is the ability to **declare each Lora knob as a `List` or a `Range`** instead of a single scalar value.  

- This lets you define a *base set of hyper‑parameter combinations* (e.g., `r=List([16, 32])`, `lora_alpha=List([16, 32])`) that RapidFire can expand into a full config group for multi‑config runs.  
- Apart from this multi‑config capability, all other semantics, defaults, and validation are inherited directly from the underlying `peft.LoraConfig`.  

So, RFLoraConfig extends LoraConfig by supporting list‑ or range‑valued arguments to enable systematic exploration of LoRA adapter variations.

**RFModelConfig** is the single object that brings together all of the pieces needed to define a model‑training run:

* **Model loading** – the `model_name` (and optional `tokenizer`/`tokenizer_kwargs`) that are passed to Hugging Face’s `AutoModel.from_pretrained()` / `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained()`.  
* **Data preprocessing** – a user‑provided `formatting_func` that prepares each example (system prompt, roles, etc.).  
* **Evaluation** – a `compute_metrics` callable that is forwarded to the Hugging Face `Trainer.compute_metrics` hook.  
* **Fine‑tuning (PEFT)** – an optional `peft_config` (e.g., `RFLoraConfig`) that wraps `peft.LoraConfig`.  
* **Training flow** – a `training_args` object (`RFSFTConfig`, `RFDPOConfig` or `RFGRPOConfig`) that controls the trainer’s hyper‑parameters and schedule.

The note clarifies that a single `RFModelConfig` may contain **only one** base model configuration and **one** training‑control‑flow arguments dictionary, while allowing lists for the other knobs (PEFT configs, formatting functions, metric functions, etc.) in a multi‑config specification.

The two arguments that are given `List` values in the example are:

- **`learning_rate`**
- **`lr_scheduler_type`**
The lite FSDP notebooks enable parameter offloading (`offload_params=True`), whereas the larger‑model FSDP notebooks turn it off (`offload_params=False`).
The example varies the **`beta`** parameter by assigning it a `List([0.1, 0.001])`.

RFvLLMModelConfig recommends that the **model_config** dictionary at least include the following keys:

- **`"model"`** – the Hugging Face model name or path (e.g., `"Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"`).  
- **`"dtype"`** – the data type for weights/activations (e.g., `"half"`, `"float"`, `"bfloat16"`).  
- **`"distributed_executor_backend"`** – the backend for distributed workers (`"ray"` or `"mp"`; only `"mp"` is currently supported).  
- **`"max_model_len"`** – the model’s context length (prompt + output). If omitted, vLLM derives it from the model config.

As RapidFire AI processes additional shards, the confidence‑interval bounds **shrink**—the intervals become tighter around the metric estimate. When the run has seen 100 % of the data (all shards processed), the intervals converge to zero width, yielding exact point‑estimate metrics.

In the example, the **traditional batch run** would take  

* 16 configs × 400 queries × 10 s/query ≈ **17.8 hours**  

whereas RapidFire AI’s online‑aggregation execution finishes in  

* **3.8 hours**  

—a **≈ 4.7× speed‑up**. (When run on 10 parallel machines the times become ~107 min vs. ~23 min, showing the same proportional gain.)
